opening.headline: Learn how to read the GDPR's definitions, principles, data subject rights, processor obligations, and impact assessments in relation to data flows from AI services.
body: Suppose a customer sends me an email asking me to provide all of their personal information and to delete my conversation history. AI services are intertwined with conversation logs, memory, analytics data, search indexes, and external providers, so it can be easy to not know where to start.

In this lesson, we will look at the definition and scope of Article 4, the principles of Article 5, response to rights requests in Articles 12 to 19, processor obligations in Article 28, and impact assessment (DPIA) in Article 35. We then analyze where each clause is connected to the AI ​​service flow.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the definitions, principles, rights, processor obligations, and DPIA of GDPR
You can distinguish the types of rights requests coming from AI services and analyze the scope of influence.

labels: Please tell me all my information

paragraphs: One day, a customer sends two emails. One is a request to provide all of my personal information, and the other is a request to delete my conversation history. This service has generative AI capabilities.

There are several places where personal information resides in AI services. Contains conversation logs, user memory, analytics data, search indexes, and archives from external providers. It can easily become unclear how much of our responsibility lies with the provider, and within what time frame and to what extent we should respond.

The GDPR stipulates how to respond to such requests. However, the condolence statement can only be read if you know the structure of the service. Each condolence message corresponds to a point in the service flow, and knowing that point allows us to answer your request accurately.
The questions for this class are: Which provisions of the GDPR are connected to which point in the AI ​​service flow?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Where should I look first if I receive a request to erase my conversation history? Answer this question again at the end of class.

screens.outro: First, let me recall my experience dealing with similar requests.

screens.title: Think of a similar situation
screens.lead: If you think about the question yourself first and then make a choice, the summary will unfold. You will not enter or submit an answer.

items.prompt: Have you ever received or received a request to view or delete personal information?
items.answer: These requests can come from anyone, regardless of size. When you first receive it, you will be confused about who is in charge and within what deadline you must respond. Establishing a request reception window and processing procedure in advance will speed up response.

items.prompt: Can I tell you at once where and how much user data is stored on your service?
items.answer: It's easy to think that you only need to find one conversation log, but in reality it often includes memory, analytical replicas, search indexes, and backups. A repository list is required to respond to all access and deletion requests.

items.prompt: Have you ever checked who is contractually responsible for what role when sending customer information to an external AI service?
items.answer: Under GDPR, the controller is the one who determines the purposes and means of processing, and the processor is the one who processes on their behalf. Duties and responsibilities vary depending on the role, so confirming the roles in the contract is a starting point.
It is not recorded. These are thought-provoking questions and will not be submitted or graded.

screens.outro: Now, let's start with the most basic definition for reading condolences.

screens.title: Article 4 Definition and scope of application
screens.lead: Explanations appear when you hover over or select key terms in the text. Think about what data in the AI ​​service each term corresponds to.

data.text: Under the GDPR, personal data means any information relating to an identified individual or an identifiable individual. It includes names, customer numbers, email addresses, locations, and browsing history. Indirect identifiers such as customer or reservation numbers are also personal data. processing covers activities such as collection, recording, storage, use, and disclosure. Non-automated processing can also be covered when the data forms part of a systematically organized filing system. Health, racial origin, political opinions, and biometric or genetic information fall within a special category; their processing is generally prohibited unless an exception such as explicit consent applies. The regulation covers organizations established in the EEA (EU countries, Iceland, Liechtenstein, and Norway), and organizations offering goods or services to, or monitoring the behavior of, individuals in the EEA. The party determining the purposes and means of processing is the controller; the party carrying out processing on its behalf is the processor. In AI services, we often assume that we are the controller and the external provider is the processor, but actual roles must be checked in the contract.

terms.tip: Even if there is no direct name, it is applicable if it can be identified by combining it with other information. Even if there is no name in the sentence in the prompt, if the person can be recognized from the context, it is a target.
All activities from collection to deletion. Processing includes logging conversations, adding them to search indexes, and sending them to external providers.

Sensitive information such as health, sex life, race/ethnicity, political opinions, religion/beliefs, labor union membership, and biometric/genetic information. You should be especially careful with services where this type of content is easily mixed, such as consultation summaries.
This is the party that determines the purpose and means of processing. The controller is responsible for responding to rights requests.
This is the side that handles processing on behalf of the controller. Process only in accordance with written instructions and assist the Controller in responding to requests.

screens.outro: Now that you know what personal data is and who has what role, let’s look at six principles that processing must follow.

screens.title: Article 5 Principles and response to AI services
screens.lead: Flip through the cards and read each principle into specific actions for the AI service. Rather than memorizing the principles as legal sentences, they will remain in your memory for a long time if you pair them with which service screens and which repositories are followed. Read the examples on the back of each card and think of one thing that might look like in your own service. The six principles also overlap with each other. For example, data minimization also reduces retention limitations and security burdens. While reading, decide on a data flow from the AI ​​service you operate or use, and try to match where this content is applied at that flow. The point where response is blocked is the area that needs to be strengthened.

cards.front: Legality, Fairness, Transparency and Article 6 Legal Basis
cards.back: The processing must have a legal basis. Article 6 sets out six grounds. These are the consent of the data subject, performance of a contract, compliance with the legal obligations of the controller, protection of vital interests such as life, public interest or exercise of official authority, and legitimate interests. In AI services, legitimate interest is often considered if the processing is necessary to provide the service, if it is for business purposes such as contract fulfillment, security, or service improvement. However, legitimate interests must undergo a review that compares them with the rights of the information subject, and the basis to use is determined separately for each purpose of processing. Transparency in informing users about how it is used is also included in this principle. The moment you turn on the AI ​​function, if your input is sent to an external provider, you will be notified of that fact.

Do not use it for new purposes that do not match the intended purpose. If you want to use the conversations collected for customer consultation for separate analysis or model improvement, you must make sure that the purpose is within the scope initially outlined.
Include only as much prompts and logs as you need for your purposes. If you don't need resident information in your summary, take a filtering step before entering it.
Inaccurate personal information will be corrected or deleted. AI-generated summaries may be subject to correction if they store incorrect information as if they were facts about people.

It is not kept in personally identifiable form longer than necessary, and is deleted or anonymized when it has served its purpose. You need to have retention policies in place for conversation logs and memory, and ensure that out-of-date data is actually erased.

Appropriate safeguards must be in place to prevent accidental or unauthorized disclosure, loss or destruction, and controllers must be able to demonstrate compliance with regulations. This includes keeping records of your settings and decisions.

screens.outro: The principles became the basis for designing services. This time, we will look at the rights that individuals have to directly request whether this principle is followed.

screens.title: Articles 12, 15, 17, and 19: Law on responding to rights requests
screens.lead: Scroll through the tabs to read what each statement asks for.

tabs.label: Types of rights and Article 12
tabs.body:
Data subjects have the rights to information, access, rectification, erasure, restriction of processing, portability, objection and the right not to be evaluated solely for automated decisions.

Article 12 sets out how to respond. Information must be provided in an easily understandable manner, and requests must be responded to within one month. If your request is complex and requires more time, we may extend the deadline by an additional two months, but you must notify us of the reason for the extension within one month of receiving your request. If we decide not to comply with your request, you will be informed of the reasons and that you have one month to file a complaint with the supervisory authority and seek judicial relief.

There is no fee for your request. However, if the request is clearly unfounded or excessively repetitive, it may be rejected or a fee may be charged, and in this case, the controller is responsible for proving the reason.

tabs.label: Article 15 Access
tabs.body:
When we receive an access request, we will confirm that we are processing that individual's information. If we are processing, we will provide you with the following information, including:
- Purpose of processing
- Recipients receiving personal information
- Retention period
- Copy of personal information

In AI services, not only conversation logs and memories, but also information sent to external providers can be included in the recipient section. So, you need to have a list of where your data flows in advance.

tabs.label: Article 17 Deletion
tabs.body:
When there are certain reasons, the information subject may request deletion. For example, if the purpose of the processing has ended, if you have withdrawn consent and there is no other legal basis, or if the processing was unlawful. However, there are exceptions, such as fulfillment of legal obligations, freedom of expression, and establishment, exercise, and defense of legal claims, so when a request is made, the grounds and exceptions must be confirmed rather than completely erased.

When applying an exception, the basis must be explained and recorded.

tabs.label: Article 19 Recipient Notification
tabs.body: Recipients who have already received the data must also be informed if correction, erasure or restriction of processing has been carried out. However, there are exceptions in cases where reporting is impossible or requires excessive effort. If there is data sent to an external AI provider, you must take steps to notify the provider or request deletion. This obligation cannot be met without a list of recipients.

screens.outro: Now that we know who responds to rights requests, let’s look at Article 28, which divides roles with external providers, and Article 35, which deals with prior evaluation.

screens.title: Article 28 Processor Obligations and Article 35 DPIA
screens.lead: Follow the steps in order to use processors and assess the impact before starting high-risk processing. Processor obligations and impact assessment are separate provisions, but in services that use external AI providers, they meet in one flow. If you check both things at the time of choosing a provider, you can save yourself the trouble of revising the contract later. Read along to find out who is responsible for each step. While reading, decide on a data flow from the AI ​​service you operate or use, and try to match where this content is applied at that flow. The point where response is blocked is the area that needs to be strengthened.

steps.title: Step 1. Choose a processor that provides sufficient coverage
steps.body: Pursuant to Article 28, controllers must only use processors that provide sufficient guarantees. When choosing an external AI provider, checking the level of security and privacy protection is a selection criterion.

steps.title: Step 2. Set scope and instructions through contract
steps.body: The scope and instructions of processing are determined by contract. Processors must only process in accordance with written instructions and must adhere to confidentiality and security measures.

steps.title: Step 3. Control subprocessors
steps.body: If the processor wants to use another company again, approval is required. If your external AI provider uses another cloud or service as a subprocessor, you should check the list and change notification method.

steps.title: Step 4. Prepare for rights requests and termination
steps.body: The processor assists the controller in responding to rights requests and deletes or returns the data at the end of the contract. Responsibility for response still lies with the controller.

steps.title: Step 5. If it is high risk, do DPIA first.
steps.body: Article 35 requires an impact assessment to be carried out before commencing processing where a high risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals is expected. Examples include large-scale special category processing, profiling-based systematic evaluations with legal or equivalent effects, and large-scale systematic monitoring of public locations. The assessment includes a description and purpose of the processing, its necessity and proportionality, risks to individual rights and measures to address those risks. The EDPB guide recommends rights request procedures and documentation even for small organizations.

screens.outro: Now, let’s put the condolences so far on top of the AI service flow.

screens.title: Corresponding article-specific obligations to AI service flow
screens.lead: When you select a marked passage in the text, the connection between the article and service point it refers to is explained. The phrases shown all refer to specific points in the service flow. While reading, decide on a data flow from the AI ​​service you operate or use, and try to match where this content is applied at that flow. The point where response is blocked is the area that needs to be strengthened.

data.text: During the collection stage, compliance with the legality and purpose limitation stipulated in Article 5, and the guidance specified in Articles 13 and 14 is observed. During the input and processing stage, data minimization as per Reduce unnecessary personal information from prompts is maintained, and agreements are established with external service providers under Article 28 Processor Agreement. During the storage stage, retention limitations and security measures are implemented, and readiness for responding to rights requests is ensured under Know where your data is. Upon receiving a rights request, the provisions of Article 12 regarding time limits, Article 15 regarding access, Article 17 regarding deletion, and Article 19 Recipient Notification are followed. If a high risk is assessed during the design stage, DPIA is carried out in accordance with Article 35. is applied. Each provision corresponds to a specific point in the service flow; understanding these points is necessary to properly respond to requests.

marks.span: Reduce unnecessary personal information from prompts
marks.note: This is a method of practicing the data minimization principle at the input stage. The best protection is not to put one in in the first place.
If the external AI provider is the processor, the contract should include the scope and direction of processing, sub-processors, and deletion or return upon termination.
In order to respond to access and deletion requests, we must first have a repository list. If you don't know the location, you won't be able to answer within the deadline.
After you make the correction or deletion, you must also notify recipients who have already received the data. A representative example is data sent to external providers.

marks.span: DPIA is carried out in accordance with Article 35.
marks.note: High-risk treatments are assessed for impact before they begin. This is during the design phase, not after the service is launched.

screens.outro: Now that we've connected the condolences and the flow, let's look at an example of how far a deletion request actually reaches.

screens.title: Commentary: Impact of deletion requests on logs, memory, and training data
screens.lead: See step-by-step how a deletion request can reach five different parts of our service. The key to this case is that a request hits multiple repositories, so be sure to check which repository it refers to at each step. While reading, decide on a data flow from the AI ​​service you operate or use, and try to match where this content is applied at that flow. The point where response is blocked is the area that needs to be strengthened.

steps.title: Step 1. draw a map
steps.body: The place where personal information resides is divided into five sections. These are conversation logs, user memory, analytics and audit logs, search indexes and embeddings, and provider-side archiving and training data. The deletion of Article 17 touches any place where an individual can be identified.

steps.title: Step 2. Delete our repository first.
steps.body: Chat logs and user memory are under our control, so they are the first things to be cleared. Search indexes and embeddings can easily remain even if the original text is deleted, so you should also remove the corresponding items from the index.

steps.title: Step 3. Write down the grounds for exception where you need to leave it.
steps.body: There are places where it is a legal obligation to leave information, such as audit logs. These areas will not be deleted, but document the exception grounds for leaving them. The requester will also be notified of the fact and reason.

steps.title: Step 4. Notify the provider or request deletion.
steps.body: For data stored by external providers, we notify the recipient in accordance with Article 19 or request contractual deletion. If you check in advance how long the provider will keep it, you can use it in your response.

steps.title: Step 5. Know the limitations of data used for learning
steps.body: It may be difficult to delete data that has already been used for model training on an individual basis. The European Personal Data Protection Board's (EDPB) opinion on AI models (Opinion 28/2024) states that models trained with personal information cannot be automatically considered anonymous, and that it must be judged on a case-by-case basis whether the possibility of extracting information about individuals from the training data or obtaining it through queries is trivial. In other words, this problem does not end with just saying that it is difficult; it is a problem that requires evidence to determine whether the model contains personal information. Therefore, it is important to confirm from the beginning the conditions that will not be used for learning in the contract and settings. It is more realistic to prevent deletion in advance rather than solving it after the fact.

screens.outro: Deletion is one of several types. Next, let's look at how to classify the types of requests.

ext.title: EDPB, Opinion 28/2024 on certain data protection aspects related to the processing of personal data in the context of AI models

screens.title: Explanation: Distinction between access, deletion, objection and automated decision requests
screens.lead: When a request comes in, we first determine what type it is and decide on a response. Compare in the table. As you read each line, think about where in the service the information you need to respond is located. While reading, decide on a data flow from the AI ​​service you operate or use, and try to match where this content is applied at that flow. The point where response is blocked is the area that needs to be strengthened.

data.caption: The key to responding by request type
rows: What personal information do we process?
We inform you of the information being processed, its purpose, recipients, retention period, and provide a copy.
Is there a reason for deletion and are there any exceptions?
Check and erase grounds and exceptions, and notify recipients who have already received them.

Objection can be exercised to processing on grounds of public interest or legitimate interest, and will stop or limit processing unless the controller can demonstrate compelling legitimate grounds. Determine the stopping range and notify
Is the decision to have legal effects or other equally significant effects solely through automated processing, or is there human intervention?

You have the right not to be subject to such decisions, except where it is necessary for the performance of a contract, permitted by law, or with your express consent. Even in exceptions, we guide you through the process for human intervention and re-examination.
notes: All requests are subject to a 1 month deadline (extendable by 2 months if complex), free of charge basis and record keeping. Even though the request type is different, these three are the same. However, requests that are clearly unfounded or excessively repeated may be subject to a reasonable fee or rejected, and in this case, the controller must prove the reason.

In cases where decisions with legal consequences or significant implications, such as loan review, are made solely through automated processing, requests to object to automated decisions will be treated differently than requests for deletion. Rather than simply giving them a copy, you should guide them through the review process.

The first column of the table is the first item to be sorted by the person receiving the request. Since the same person may request access and deletion in the same email, dividing requests by type and managing deadlines for each reduces the number of missed requests. When there is reasonable doubt about the requester's identity, additional information may be requested to verify this, so this process should also be included in the application process, and care must be taken not to collect more personal information than is necessary during the verification process. Response records serve as evidence that the regulations have been followed.

screens.outro: Now that we've outlined how to classify requests, let's finally look at the order of checking the role when using an external AI provider.

ext.title: GDPR Art. 22, Automated individual decision-making, including profiling

screens.title: Commentary: Checking the division of roles when using an external AI provider
screens.lead: Open each item one by one and read the order and rationale for confirmation. It is recommended that the inspection be repeated before signing the contract and upon renewal. If you write down the supporting documents for each item, you can immediately answer questions from supervisory authorities or clients. While reading, decide on a data flow from the AI ​​service you operate or use, and try to match where this content is applied at that flow. The point where response is blocked is the area that needs to be strengthened.

items.title: 1. Verify that we are the controller and the provider is the processor
items.body: Check who determines the purposes and means of processing in the contract. If the provider processes the data sent to us on our instructions for the purpose of providing services, we are usually the controller and the provider is the processor. If the roles are written differently, you need to find out why.

items.title: 2. Make sure the scope and instructions are documented
items.body: Processors will only process in accordance with written instructions. The contract must specify which data will be processed and for what purpose, as well as how to change the instructions.

items.title: 3. Check the list of sub-processors and change notification method
items.body: Approval is required to use another provider. Find out if the list of subprocessors is public, how you will be notified when it changes, and whether you can object.

items.title: 4. When a request for rights is made, check the procedures and deadlines provided by the provider.
items.body: The controller is responsible for responding to rights requests, and the processor assists in this. You must know in advance the process and time required to find or delete data stored at the provider so that you can respond within the one-month deadline.

items.title: 5. If it is a high-risk use, first determine whether DPIA is necessary.
items.body: If your purpose is to cover large special categories or evaluate people based on profiling, determine whether an impact assessment is needed before launching the service. Record the results and basis for your judgment.

screens.outro: Now that we have completed the review of roles, we will organize the contents of this class into one.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: Let's combine the condolences and service flow responses covered in this class into one framework. Answer the reflection questions yourself, but do not record or submit your answers. Among the condolences learned today, choose one thing to check first in the service.

paragraphs: Article 4 broadens the scope of personal data and processing and provides separate protection for special categories. The six principles in Article 5, such as data minimization and retention limits, serve as the basis for service design.

Articles 12, 15, 17 and 19 establish the time limit and scope for responding to requests and notification of recipients. Article 28 requires contracts and instructions when using processors, and Article 35 requires prior assessment of high-risk processing. These provisions are not items to be memorized separately, but rather inspection items attached to each point of the service flow.
In summary, you must know where a person's personal information is stored and to whom it is transmitted, so that all provisions can be kept. The data map is the starting point for all obligations.

If you transfer the correspondence table created in this class to a service document, you can immediately find which clauses need to be rechecked every time you add a new function. It is important to have the habit of modifying the data map when functions change.

glossary.def: Any information about an identified or identifiable individual
The party that determines the purpose and means of processing and the party that processes it on their behalf
Rights exercised by individuals over their own information, such as access, correction, deletion, portability, and opposition.
Data protection impact assessment before commencing processing where high risk is expected
The principle of processing personal information only as necessary for the purpose
There are six bases that must exist for the processing of personal data to be lawful: consent, performance of a contract, legal obligation, vital interest, public interest and legitimate interest.

misconceptions.myth: A pseudonym or customer number is not personal information.
misconceptions.fact: Indirect identification is also personal information.

misconceptions.myth: Rights requests are handled by the processor provider.
misconceptions.fact: Responsibility for response lies with the controller and the processor assists in this.

misconceptions.myth: If a request for deletion is received, all information must be deleted.
misconceptions.fact: There are exceptions, such as legal preservation obligations, but they must be justified.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Articles 4 and 5 establish the objects and principles.
Rights requests will be responded to free of charge within one month and the recipient will be notified.
The processor assists the controller in accordance with the contract and instructions.
For high-risk processing, DPIA is performed first.
